Pervasiveness of dynasties in Congress, neighboring countries, business, professions, and ordinary families

stances.claim: Congress has never defined political dynasties because the presidency and Congress have always been dominated by dynasties -- the electorate placed them there with full knowledge of lineage and pedigree.
Every Philippine president under the 1987 Constitution has been dynastic except Fidel V. Ramos -- Cory Aquino, Estrada, Arroyo, Duterte, and Marcos Jr. all anchor identifiable dynasties.
Dynasties are not evil per se -- most members are talented and well-intentioned; the conglomerate leaders CJ knows are 'patriotic, honest, fair, and philanthropic.'

Rather than chase the impossible abolition of dynasties, the better goal is to transform dynasty into legacy -- forebears leading by example and inculcating excellence, integrity, prudence, and humility in the next generation.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing maneuver from prohibition to formation

stances.claim: The populace must demand and expect dynasts to devote their full time, talent, and resources to abolishing extreme poverty, taming inflation, protecting sovereignty, safeguarding liberty, and nurturing prosperity under the rule of law.
stances.rhetorical_move: civic-demand counterweight to the legacy frame

stances.claim: Abolishing dynasties is even more impossible than transforming them -- they are 'in the historical genes' of the Filipino people and of many parts of the world.

one_paragraph_summary: Provoked by the Cha-cha hearings, Panganiban turns the dynasty debate from prohibition to formation. He sides with framer Christian Monsod that Congress should first discharge its long-ignored mandate under Article II, Section 26 to define political dynasties -- but answers his own question on why it has never done so: the presidency and Congress have always been dominated by dynasties, placed there knowingly by the electorate. He inventories every Philippine president since 1987 -- all dynastic except Fidel V. Ramos -- naming the Aquino, Estrada, Arroyo, Duterte, and Marcos lineages, and observes that Congress is 'littered with dynasties' (Villars, Cayetanos, Binays, Gatchalians) without calling them 'evil per se.' He widens the lens: Thailand venerates its king under lèse-majesté, Japan its emperor with God-like reverence, Malaysia its sultans and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong. Business conglomerates such as Ayala have succeeded by training their heirs; physicians and lawyers want their children to inherit their practices; ordinary elders want their heirs to absorb 'native ways and folksy wisdom.' He discloses that he dreamed of transmitting his Chief Justice legacy to his heirs but, since none became lawyers, he formed the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity to perpetuate his legacy and philosophy. His thesis: dynasts are here to stay -- 'in the historical genes' of the Filipino people -- so the better course is to transform dynasty into legacy, with forebears leading by example and inculcating in the next generation 'the culture of excellence, integrity, prudence, and humility,' preparing them not only for the here and now but for the hereafter. The civic counterweight is equally important: the populace must demand and expect dynasts to devote 'their full time, talent, and resources to abolish extreme poverty, tame inflation, protect our sovereignty, safeguard liberty, and nurture prosperity under the rule of law.' Transforming dynasty into legacy may seem impossible, he dares say -- but abolishing dynasties is even more so.
